q: We autoscaled during a traffic spike and now the whole database is refusing new connections for every service, not just the one we scaled up — what's supposed to stop that?
note: Tests recall of the shared-external-pooler ruling as the fix for per-process pools multiplying past max_connections during scale-out; phrased around the outage symptom, not pooling vocabulary.

q: Nightly backups are creeping past their window and barely finish before the next one kicks off — could old deleted rows we never actually clean up be the reason?
note: Targets the later hard-purge-after-retention-window note on soft-vs-hard-delete, not the original soft-delete-only ruling; framed as a backup-performance symptom to avoid 'soft delete'/'retention' vocabulary and to test recency over the axis's first ruling. backup-restore-testing is a plausible but wrong near-miss since it's also about backups.

q: If the process crashes right after we respond to a request, is there any guarantee something got logged about what just happened?
note: Gold axis's own later notes PARK the synchronous guarantee (no transactional sink, buffered-in-memory, lost on crash) — the honest answer is 'no, not currently', which the retrieved axis must surface rather than the original ruling alone. audit-trail-retention is a tempting but wrong near-miss (it's about retention duration, not delivery guarantees).

q: Is it fine for our nightly billing reconciliation job to query the follower database, or could that show numbers that lag behind what's actually true?
note: Uses 'follower database' instead of 'replica'/'readFrom flag' to avoid the ruling's vocabulary; money-adjacent job makes the prohibited-flag nuance relevant. cache-invalidation-ownership is a plausible distractor since it's also about stale-data races between services.

q: When someone resets their password after a suspected account takeover, does the attacker's existing browser session die immediately, or just whenever it was already going to expire?
note: Tests the immediate-revocation-on-password-change ruling; session-store is a strong sibling-axis distractor (same subject, different concern — where sessions live vs. when they die).

q: We've got dozens of toggles nobody remembers enabling, and nobody can say which code paths behind them are even reachable anymore. Is there a cleanup policy for this?
note: Matches the 30-day-rollout-then-delete ruling; phrased around the symptom (unreachable dead branches) rather than the rule's own wording.

q: A page fired for a system that doesn't clearly belong to any team on the rotation, and it bounced around forever before anyone could act on it. Shouldn't every alert have to name a team up front?
note: Directly tests the mandatory-owning-team-at-creation ruling; incident-severity-definitions is a plausible near-miss since both concern incident-response process gaps.

q: If a hardcoded key baked into one service's config ever leaked, could someone use it to impersonate that service when calling our other internal systems? What's meant to rule that out entirely?
note: Tests the mutual-TLS-over-static-keys ruling for internal service calls; third-party-token-custody is a deliberate mutual distractor (also about credential leak blast-radius, but for external vendor tokens, not internal service identity).

q: We're mid-incident. Fastest way back online is to build off yesterday's code and push that out — does someone else still need to approve the deploy first?
note: Two independent clauses, each settled by a different axis: (1) building fresh from source and shipping it is exactly the rebuild path the rollback axis forbids — a real rollback must redeploy the prior artifact's exact digest — and (2) the approval axis separately says there is no emergency bypass for sign-off. Neither axis alone answers both halves of the question.

q: It's urgent tonight — can we flip the new version on for all traffic in one go, and skip finding someone else to sign off since there's no time?
note: The 'all traffic in one go' clause is settled by the traffic-ramp axis (single-flip is reserved for schema-incompatible deploys only), and the 'skip sign-off' clause is settled by the separate no-bypass approval axis. Both rulings are independently violated by the proposal, so both are required to give a complete answer.

q: Legal wants a customer's data completely gone today per a request — realistically, is anything about them going to stick around anywhere for years regardless?
note: The delete axis says the row goes soft-delete immediately but only hard-purges on a scheduled job after a ~400-day window (and only if not under legal hold) — so 'gone today' is already false on that axis alone. Separately, the retention axis says privileged-action audit records (auth events, permission grants, regulated-data access) touching that account are retained 7 years, immutable, exempt from any purge. Both rulings are needed to answer 'is anything left, and for how long.'

q: After a forced sign-out, is there anywhere in the stack an old token could still sneak through, and where would we even look to check?
note: The invalidation axis answers whether an old token could still work (no — every request is checked against a revocation list, not just decoded and trusted). The store axis answers where that check and the underlying session data actually live (a dedicated cache keyed by session id, with a database read-through on miss) — which is what 'where would we look' is actually asking. Answering only one leaves either the guarantee or the location unaddressed.

q: How long before an unacknowledged page escalates to a secondary responder?
note: Adjacent to alert-ownership, which rules on WHO an alert's owning team is and that pages route only to that team's rotation. It says nothing about escalation timing or a secondary-contact SLA once a page goes unacknowledged — that facet is left open.

q: If legal orders a takedown of an old release binary, are we allowed to delete it from where it's stored?
note: Adjacent to artifact-immutability, which forbids overwriting/republishing an existing version tag. Outright deletion/takedown of an artifact is a different operation from overwrite and is never addressed; rollback-mechanism's registry-retention note is about automatic GC windows for rollback eligibility, not manual/legal deletion.

q: Does an outgoing webhook to a customer need to finish delivering before we send back the HTTP response?
note: Adjacent to audit-log-delivery, which rules (and is currently PARKED/unimplemented for) internal audit-event delivery only. Outbound customer-facing webhook delivery is a distinct data path never mentioned in that or any other axis.

q: How long do we have to keep customer support chat transcripts around?
note: Adjacent to audit-trail-retention, whose narrowed ruling covers only privileged-action records (auth events, permission grants, regulated-data access). Ordinary support chat transcripts don't fall in that carved-out category, so the 7-year/90-day split doesn't settle them.

q: What algorithm decides when we've hit capacity and start turning requests away?
note: Adjacent to backpressure-shedding, which rules THAT overload is shed at admission with a 503, not HOW admission decides capacity is exceeded. The specific algorithm (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window, etc.) is never specified.

q: How often do we run a full failover drill against our disaster-recovery region?
note: Adjacent to backup-restore-testing, which rules on restoring a backup onto a scratch instance to verify it's usable. A live cross-region DR failover drill is a different exercise (routing traffic to a standby region) that this axis never covers.

q: How long should a cached entry sit before it expires on its own?
note: Adjacent to cache-invalidation-ownership, which settles WHO may write or invalidate a cache key (the owning service, via namespace prefix), not how long an entry should live before natural expiration. TTL duration is a separate, unaddressed facet.

q: When we ship a new mobile app build to the App Store, do we stagger it out to users gradually or release to everyone at once?
note: Adjacent to canary-vs-blue-green, whose ruling is scoped to deploy/** backend service deploys and their traffic-percentage canary steps. Mobile releases go through app-store review and store-side staged rollout, a channel this axis never addresses.

q: What's the rule for sizing the shared connection pooler's cap so it can't blow past the database's connection ceiling again?
note: Adjacent to connection-pooling: the axis's own trailing note explicitly flags this exact sizing question as an unresolved, moved risk ('the risk moved, it did not disappear') without giving a formula or resolved cap — the corpus deliberately leaves it open.

q: When someone leaves the company, how fast does their service account access get pulled?
note: Adjacent to least-privilege-defaults, which rules on the DEFAULT permission set at account provisioning time (zero permissions, one pre-granted namespace), not on deprovisioning speed when someone leaves. session-invalidation covers session token revocation on password change/attack, not offboarding access removal — neither settles this.

q: What's the actual timeout value we set on an inbound API call before we give up on it?
note: Adjacent to request-timeout-policy, which rules THAT every inbound request carries an absolute deadline and is cancelled rather than queued when it outlives it — but never states a concrete duration/value for that deadline anywhere in the corpus.

q: One of our requests fans out to like eight other services in a row and comes back clean, no errors. If it doesn't happen to land in the sampling percentage, is the full path still saved somewhere, or is it just gone?
note: The Target ruling (target:2026-02-18) promises any request fanning out past five services is guaranteed captured in full via a tail-based collector override, independent of head-sampling odds. Its own later notes on that same block say the collector can't actually buffer at current traffic, the override is PARKED, and by 2026-05-20 the fan-out guarantee is explicitly aspirational: a large fan-out request that wasn't head-sampled or errored is captured exactly like any other successful request, probabilistically, not guaranteed. Returning the Target ruling alone gives a confident yes that is currently false.

mustNotAssert: guaranteed to be captured in full

q: Is it basically down to each engineer to remember not to point a payments query at a replica, or is there something underneath that stops it even if they get that wrong?
note: The Target ruling (target:2026-02-09) makes replica routing opt-in per query via a caller-set flag, banning that flag on money and entitlement paths, so the safety mechanism is caller discipline. Its own later note says this was FALSIFIED in part: a session-affinity bug replayed a caller's later default reads through a replica connection it had just opted into, so enforcement was moved into the query builder itself, which now rejects a replica flag on any money or entitlement query regardless of what the caller passed. Caller discipline is explicitly no longer the enforcement mechanism, so an answer that says routing safety still depends on the caller remembering to opt in is stale.

mustSurface: caller discipline is no longer the enforcement mechanism
mustNotAssert: Replica routing is opt-in per query

q: If someone throws together a dashboard panel during an incident, is that panel actually still going to be there next month?
note: The Target ruling (target:2026-04-08) locks dashboards to version-controlled JSON with a read-only UI everywhere except a designated scratch sandbox, so incident-time edits outside it get silently overwritten on the next deploy. The later note says the sandbox itself became a dumping ground: responders build panels there but rarely promote them back into source, so useful panels still vanish once it is periodically reset, the exact read-only and panel-loss problem the ruling was meant to solve has resurfaced one layer over. Answering as if using the sandbox now safely preserves incident panels is stale.

mustNotAssert: any edit made outside that sandbox is overwritten without warning on the next deploy

q: We log every time someone views a customer's profile as an audit event. Do those particular records stick around for years too, or do they eventually get cleared out like ordinary logs?
note: The Target ruling (target:2026-03-22) puts every audit trail entry, including data access broadly, into 7-year, immutable, rotation-exempt storage. A later note has legal counsel narrow that: only privileged-action records, auth events, permission grants, access to regulated data, actually carry the 7-year obligation; ordinary read-traffic audit entries that do not touch regulated data revert to the standard 90-day rotation. A plain read of an ordinary customer profile is exactly the kind of read-traffic entry that no longer gets the 7-year or rotation-exempt treatment, so citing the original blanket ruling for it is now wrong.

mustSurface: only the privileged-action subset carries a retention obligation
mustNotAssert: authentication events, permission grants, and data access
exempt from the standard log-rotation TTL that governs everything else

q: We keep some of our signing keys on physical hardware tokens. Do those get swapped out automatically every month along with everything else, or are they on a different clock?
note: The Target ruling (target:2026-01-25) puts every service and integration secret, explicitly including signing keys, on an automatic fixed 30-day rotation with no manual skip path. A later note carves out hardware-backed signing keys entirely: rotating them needs a manual ceremony with a physical token that cannot be automated that tightly, so those specific keys rotate quarterly during a planned maintenance window instead, while every other secret class stays on the automatic 30-day cycle. Answering that signing keys held on hardware tokens still auto-rotate every 30 days like the rest is stale for that subset.

mustSurface: Hardware-backed signing keys are exempted from the 30-day cycle
Those keys rotate quarterly during a planned maintenance window instead
mustNotAssert: rotated automatically by the secrets manager on a fixed 30-day cycle

q: If a customer asks us to delete their data, does it ever actually come out of the database, or does it just sit there marked deleted forever?
note: The first Target block (target:2026-01-25) rules that deletes are soft-only forever, with no application code path ever permitted to hard-delete a row, the only exit being a one-off reviewed operational script. That block was superseded by a second Target (target:2026-05-11): a scheduled job now automatically hard-deletes rows whose deleted_at is past the retention window (default 400 days) after a legal-hold check, so rows do leave the database on a routine, non-manual path. Answering with the first block's soft-delete-forever framing states a guarantee that no longer holds.

mustSurface: after checking each row against an active legal-hold table
mustNotAssert: the only way a row leaves the database is through an explicitly reviewed, one-off operational script
